opus-5.5.text:
For me, mathematics isn't just the domain we work in. It's the way we think about everything we build.

Mathematics is the one field where truth is absolute. A proof is either correct or it isn't. There's no "mostly right," no vibes, no persuasion. That standard of rigor is incredibly rare, and I think it's exactly what AI needs right now. Today's models are amazing at producing things that *look* right: fluent text, plausible code, convincing arguments. But looking right and being right are very different. Mathematics, especially formal mathematics in systems like Lean, gives you a way to close that gap. You can check every step mechanically. So when we say math is our DNA, part of it means building systems where correctness is verifiable, not just claimed.

The second part is culture. Many people on our team came up through math olympiads, research mathematics, or theoretical computer science. Doing math trains a particular temperament: you sit with a hard problem for weeks, you get stuck, you're wrong most of the time, and you learn to love that process because the breakthrough at the end is so clean. That patience and honesty about what you actually know shapes how we do research and make decisions as a company. We try not to fool ourselves.

The third part is mission. I genuinely believe mathematics is a kind of foundation layer for reasoning itself. If you can build an AI that can reliably discover and verify new mathematics, you've built something that reasons, not something that just pattern-matches. And the downstream impact is huge: verified software, chip design, cryptography, physics, anywhere you need guarantees rather than guesses.

So mathematics is what we work on, it's how we work, and it's why we think this matters. That's why I call it our DNA.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I say mathematics is our DNA, I mean it quite literally rather than as a slogan. I grew up doing math, I trained as a mathematician, and when I started Axiom, the question I kept asking was not "what product can we ship" but "what is actually true, and how do we know it."

Mathematics is the one domain where that question has a hard answer. A proof is either valid or it is not. There is no partial credit, no persuasive hallucination. That makes it the most honest training ground for AI reasoning you can imagine. If a model can produce a formally verified proof, you do not have to trust it. You can check it. And that property, verifiability, is what I think the whole field is missing right now.

So mathematics shapes everything about how we work. It shapes what we build, which is systems that reason toward verifiable truth rather than plausible text. It shapes who we hire. Many of our people are olympiad medalists or research mathematicians, and they bring a certain intolerance for hand-waving that is very healthy in an AI company. And it shapes our culture. We argue the way mathematicians argue, which means the argument ends when someone produces a proof, not when someone with more seniority gets tired.

There is also a personal dimension. Math was how I first learned to think, and it was how I learned that being wrong is not shameful, it is just information. I want the company to carry that. If the DNA is mathematical, then the company inherits that humility and that rigor, and I believe that is what it takes to build something that will still be standing when the hype cycle moves on.

astra-6.text:
I see mathematics as our DNA because it shapes how we approach problems. You start by asking: What are the assumptions? What exactly are we trying to establish? And does each step of the reasoning actually hold up?

That’s especially valuable when you’re building AI. There’s a difference between producing an answer that sounds convincing and producing one you can trust. Mathematics gives us a way to think rigorously about that gap.

And it’s also a creative discipline. You explore, try different approaches, and look for a simple idea that makes a difficult problem clearer. That combination of imagination and rigor is what I want at the heart of the company.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, mathematics is a way of thinking: you start with a difficult problem, make your assumptions explicit, and work toward a solution you can justify. That’s the mindset I want at the heart of our company.

It also shapes how we approach AI. We want to understand why something works, where it breaks, and how to make it more reliable. Mathematics gives us a language for asking those questions precisely. So when I call it our DNA, I mean it influences both what we build and how we make decisions.
